name: Ray & Porcell
label: Revelation
lede: Two songs, a ten-dollar drum machine and one black-and-white photo of two straight edge icons staring out a Manhattan window, which ended up outliving the music.

eras.title: Track 4 on a four-track
eras.text: Youth of Today had just finished its first run, Ray Cappo had joined a temple and was sleeping at John "Porcell" Porcelly's apartment, and the New York scene was changing around them. Porcell had been messing with a sampler and a drum machine, and wanted to write something that sounded nothing like Youth of Today.

years.p: Porcell records a rough electronic demo on a sampler, sequencer and drum machine, and names it for where it sits on his 4-track cassette. Dylan Schreifels, Walter Schreifels's younger brother, helps him arrange it.
years.xp: Porcell said everything in the NYHC scene was changing, and that [[Quicksand|3c9f8bef-a658-4204-9ee8-7e95d2535b32]] coming up made him want to experiment. The touchstones were [[Dag Nasty|4709dd69-1034-4634-9e88-d1099453b192]], [[Embrace|9d1ad8e3-8740-429a-bdc5-52f96a9c4431]], '80s Iggy Pop and the Sisters of Mercy.

years.h: Ray Cappo writes lyrics on the spot, before leaving for India
years.p: Staying at Porcell's place after joining a temple and before a trip to India, Ray Cappo writes the words and melodies for Porcell's two songs, Fame and Broken Glass, quickly and spontaneously.

years.h: Ray & Porcell record at [[Don Fury|0bec484f-b890-4823-af64-0e48530f6f6f]]'s with a $10 drum machine
years.p: No drummer: the beat comes from a drum machine Porcell bought for about $10 in Manhattan's Music District. Ray Cappo sings, Porcell plays everything else.
years.xp: Revelation's Jordan Cooper says the whole 7" grew out of Porcell's little electronic demo, and that he had to keep at a reluctant Porcell to put it out. Porcell didn't want to call it Ray and Porcell either; the name was a suggestion that stuck.

eras.title: Two faces in a window
eras.text: Revelation pressed 5,000 copies of a two-song record with no drummer and no hardcore tempo. Kids either loved it or hated it, and the cover photo turned into something bigger than both songs.

years.p: Fame and Broken Glass. Revelation's first pressing is 4,000 on black vinyl and 1,000 on purple.
years.xp: A second, final pressing of just 100 on black came in photocopied, hand-numbered sleeves. RevHQ has since reissued it on opaque blue, 550 copies.

years.p: Photographer Raymond Legenzowski, who'd shot for Nike, catches Ray Cappo and Porcell gazing out a window in a downtown Manhattan office building. Most of his other frames from that day are lost.
years.xp: The picture outlived the record. The clothing brand Wear Dinner built merch around it and went as far as declaring an International Ray & Porcell 7" Day.

years.big: Love it or hate it. Porcell didn't care which.
q: I've never been terribly concerned with other people's opinion of me.
years.h: Hardcore kids split over the Ray & Porcell 7"
years.p: Fans of Ray Cappo and Porcell's old band [[Youth of Today|9ca27db4-f127-4aeb-ae87-29e21f558c13]] either loved the drum machine songs or rejected them outright. Porcell shrugged it off.

years.h: Ray Cappo and Porcell move on to [[Shelter|d5157104-76b1-4b8b-90c2-9ff994f940db]] and [[Judge|3827fbb6-e219-4e2d-9af8-35cc9a7d8d8e]]
years.p: Ray Cappo puts his Krishna-conscious hardcore into [[Shelter|d5157104-76b1-4b8b-90c2-9ff994f940db]], and Porcell plays with him there after [[Judge|3827fbb6-e219-4e2d-9af8-35cc9a7d8d8e]], his band with [[Mike Ferraro|edffc714-f0a2-4d6c-b4c0-dc31e713481c]], ends in 1991.
